advances: The arbitrary-product second- and third-moment theorem for distinct pair midpoints extends to every fixed bound \(\Delta\) on the number of same-parity pairs with a common midpoint. The proof establishes a multiple-pair energy charge and score price and selects individual pairs in global dyadic ratio bands. Its constants depend only on \(\Delta\). This multiplicity parameter is unrelated to the continuous dimension \(d\) of the locked mixed-integer-volume problem. The theorem makes no general-\(H_q\) assertion and does not resolve that locked conjecture.
author: research-agent
proof:
We use ee640ebdfbcb632d only as the accepted canonical notation and distinct-midpoint predecessor. The maps for \(n,A,w,Z,p,\tau,H,b,\chi,M_2,M_3\) are the identity. All estimates needed when midpoints collide are proved below. In particular, no unique-midpoint charge from that predecessor is assumed. Hatted objects will always be auxiliary restricted reflected rows, rather than changed original laws. The auxiliary atom sum \(A_0\) introduced below is not the canonical ratio \(a(p)=\chi(p)/b(p)\).

First work in one original factor, suppress \(\ell\), and put \(K=2^n\). Let \(\mathcal P\) be the set of all unordered pairs \(e=\lbrace u_e,v_e\rbrace\) of distinct same-parity points of \(A\), with center \(j_e=(u_e+v_e)/2\). Choose either ordering of each pair. Each two-point parity class contributes exactly one pair, so distinct pairs have disjoint endpoint sets. All \(j_e\) belong to \(A\) by assumption 2, and at most \(\Delta\) pairs have any one center by assumption 3. An atom can be the center of at most \(\Delta\) pairs and an endpoint of at most one pair, and these roles may overlap. Also \(|A|\le2K\).

For each supported center \(x\), its full reflected row is exactly
$$
R_x:=\lbrace y\in A:2x-y\in A\rbrace
 =\lbrace x\rbrace\cup
 \bigcup_{e\in\mathcal P:j_e=x}\lbrace u_e,v_e\rbrace.
\tag{1}
$$
Indeed distinct reflected endpoints have equal coordinatewise parity and hence give one of the pairs in \(\mathcal P\); conversely every pair centered at \(x\) gives those two reflected endpoints. The union in (1) has no repeated endpoints, and neither endpoint of a nontrivial pair equals its own center.

For \(e\in\mathcal P\) set
$$
\begin{aligned}
s_e&=\frac{\sqrt{p_{u_e}p_{v_e}}}{p_{j_e}}\in(0,1],&
z_e&=\frac12\log\frac{p_{v_e}}{p_{u_e}},\\
\rho_e&=\log(1/s_e)\ge0,&
\beta_e&=Ks_ep_{j_e}^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
$$
The bound \(s_e\le1\) is exactly the assumed midpoint inequality. Thus the full canonical reflected sum is \(H_p(x)=p_x\bigl(1+2\sum_{e\in\mathcal P:j_e=x}s_e\bigr)\), and in particular \(p_x\le H_p(x)\le Q_\Delta p_x\).

Fix any subset \(\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal P\), with selection by individual pairs even when their centers coincide. At each supported center \(x\) retain the symmetric auxiliary row
$$
\widehat R_x=\lbrace x\rbrace\cup
 \bigcup_{e\in\mathcal S:j_e=x}\lbrace u_e,v_e\rbrace.
$$
Define
$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat H(x)&=\sum_{y\in\widehat R_x}\sqrt{p_yp_{2x-y}},&
\widehat b&=\sum_{x\in A}p_x\widehat H(x)^2,&
\widehat\chi&=\sum_{x\in A}p_x\widehat H(x),\\
\widehat\kappa_x(y)&=\frac{\sqrt{p_yp_{2x-y}}}{\widehat H(x)}
 &&(y\in\widehat R_x),\\
\widehat Y_x(y)&=\frac12\log\frac{p_y}{p_{2x-y}},&
\widehat V_x&=\mathbb E_{\widehat\kappa_x}\widehat Y_x^2,\\
\widehat q_x&=\frac{p_x\widehat H(x)^2}{\widehat b},&
\widehat\nu&=\sum_{x\in A}\widehat q_x\widehat V_x.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
$$
All sums over \(x\) here are over the entire original \(A\), and every probability is still \(p_x=w_x/Z\). No atom or normalizer is discarded. The rows are symmetric under \(y\mapsto2x-y\); consequently that map preserves \(\widehat\kappa_x\) and negates \(\widehat Y_x\), so the score has mean zero. Every row contains \(x\) and \(p_x>0\), so all denominators in (3) are positive.

Write \(h_x=1+2\sum_{e\in\mathcal S:j_e=x}s_e\), so that \(\widehat H(x)=h_xp_x\) and \(1\le h_x\le Q_\Delta\). Define the auxiliary cubic sums \(A_0=K^2\sum_{x\in A}p_x^3\) and \(A_{\mathcal S}=K^2\widehat b\). The support bound, Jensen under the uniform measure on \(A\), and \(p_x\le\widehat H(x)\le H_p(x)\le Q_\Delta p_x\) give
$$
\frac14\le A_0\le A_{\mathcal S}\le K^2b(p)\le Q_\Delta^2A_0.
\tag{4}
$$

For each of the \(K\) coordinatewise parities \(\eta\in\lbrace0,1\rbrace^n\), including empty classes, put \(r_\eta=p(\eta+2\mathbb Z^n)\). Define the nonnegative energies and pair intensities
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal D&=K\sum_\eta r_\eta^2-1
 =\frac1K\sum_\eta(Kr_\eta-1)^2,\\
\mathcal V_{\mathcal S}&=\sum_{x\in A}p_x(K\widehat H(x)-1)^2,&
\mathcal T_{\mathcal S}&=4K\sum_{e\in\mathcal S}s_e(1-s_e)p_{j_e}^2,\\
\mathcal E_{\mathcal S}&=\mathcal V_{\mathcal S}+2\mathcal D+\mathcal T_{\mathcal S},&
\beta_{\mathcal S}&=\sum_{e\in\mathcal S}\beta_e,\\
\zeta_{\mathcal S^c}&=K\sum_{e\in\mathcal P\setminus\mathcal S}s_e^2p_{j_e}^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}
$$
Here \(\mathcal V_{\mathcal S}\) is a deviation energy, distinct from the individual row score variances \(\widehat V_x\). The disjoint two-point parity classes and the definition of the selected rows give the exact identities
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_\eta r_\eta^2
 &=\sum_{x\in A}p_x^2+2\sum_{e\in\mathcal P}s_e^2p_{j_e}^2,\\
\widehat\chi
 &=\sum_{x\in A}p_x^2+2\sum_{e\in\mathcal S}s_ep_{j_e}^2,\\
\mathcal V_{\mathcal S}&=A_{\mathcal S}-2K\widehat\chi+1.
\end{aligned}
$$
Substitution yields, with no distinct-center assumption,
$$
A_{\mathcal S}=1+\mathcal E_{\mathcal S}-4\zeta_{\mathcal S^c}.
\tag{6}
$$
We prove a uniform intensity charge valid for every selection \(\mathcal S\):
$$
\beta_{\mathcal S}\le C_\Delta\mathcal E_{\mathcal S}.
\tag{7}
$$

For \(t\ge0\) and any vector \(\mathbf a=(a_1,\ldots,a_\Delta)\in[0,1]^\Delta\) define
$$
F_\Delta(t,\mathbf a)
 =t\left[\left(1+2\sum_{i=1}^\Delta a_i\right)t-1\right]^2
 +4t^2\sum_{i=1}^\Delta a_i(1-a_i).
$$
For \(0\le t\le1\) its second derivative in each individual \(a_i\) is \(8t^2(t-1)\le0\). Minimizing that coordinate on \([0,1]\) therefore permits replacement by an endpoint without increasing the value. Repeating over all coordinates shows that the minimum over the cube occurs at a vertex. A vertex with \(k\) ones has value \(t((1+2k)t-1)^2\). For \(t\ge1\) the first derivative in \(a_i\) is
$$
4t^2\left[t+2t\sum_{h\ne i}a_h+2a_i(t-1)\right]\ge0,
$$
so the minimum is attained at the all-zero vector. Since \(((1+2k)t-1)^2\ge(t-1)^2\) for \(t\ge1\) and \(k\ge0\), these two arguments prove, for every \(t\ge0\),
$$
F_\Delta(t,\mathbf a)
 \ge t\min_{0\le k\le\Delta}((2k+1)t-1)^2.
\tag{8}
$$

At each atom \(x\) take \(t_x=Kp_x\) and let \(\mathbf a(x)\) be the list of \(s_e\) for the selected pairs centered at \(x\), padded with zeros to length \(\Delta\). Put \(F_x=F_\Delta(t_x,\mathbf a(x))\). Exact accounting gives
$$
\sum_{x\in A}F_x=K(\mathcal V_{\mathcal S}+\mathcal T_{\mathcal S}).
\tag{9}
$$
This accounts for all selected pairs at the same center together, rather than treating their full row factors as independent.

For any two odd integers \(a,b\in\lbrace1,3,\ldots,Q_\Delta\rbrace\), one has
$$
\left|\frac1a+\frac1b-1\right|\ge\frac1{Q_\Delta^2}.
\tag{10}
$$
To prove this, \(a+b-ab\) is an integer. It cannot vanish, since \(a+b=ab\) would give \((a-1)(b-1)=1\), whereas the left side is divisible by four. Thus its absolute value is at least one, and \(ab\le Q_\Delta^2\). This proves (10), including repeated choices \(a=b\).

A selected pair with \(s_e\le7/8\) has \(4s_e(1-s_e)\ge s_e/2\), so the sum of \(\beta_e\) over all such pairs is at most \(2\mathcal T_{\mathcal S}\). Consider instead a selected pair with \(s=s_e>7/8\). Set \(\xi=Kp_{j_e}\), \(\upsilon=Kp_{u_e}\), \(\omega=Kp_{v_e}\), and \(\delta_e=(\upsilon+\omega-1)^2\). The product identity is \(\upsilon\omega=s^2\xi^2\). We claim
$$
s\xi^2\le256Q_\Delta^6
 \bigl(F_{j_e}+F_{u_e}+F_{v_e}+\delta_e\bigr).
\tag{11}
$$

If \(\xi\le1/(2Q_\Delta)\), then \(h_{j_e}\xi\le1/2\) and \(F_{j_e}\ge\xi/4\). Consequently \(s\xi^2\le\xi^2\le4F_{j_e}\). If \(\xi\ge4/9\), then \(h_{j_e}\ge1+2s>11/4\), hence \(h_{j_e}\xi-1\ge\xi/2\) and \(F_{j_e}\ge\xi^3/4\ge\xi^2/9\). Thus \(s\xi^2\le9F_{j_e}\). Both cases imply (11).

It remains to treat \(1/(2Q_\Delta)<\xi<4/9\). In this case \(\upsilon\omega>49/(256Q_\Delta^2)\) and \(s\xi^2<16/81<1/4\). Set \(\delta=1/(4Q_\Delta^2)\), \(a_*=1/(16Q_\Delta^2)\), and \(\varepsilon=1/(1024Q_\Delta^6)\). If \(\delta_e\ge\delta^2\), then \(\delta_e\ge\varepsilon\), since \(\delta^2/\varepsilon=64Q_\Delta^2\ge1\). Otherwise
$$
|\upsilon+\omega-1|<\delta,\qquad
\upsilon+\omega<2,\qquad
\upsilon>a_*,\quad\omega>a_*.
$$
For the last inequalities, each endpoint is greater than its product with the other divided by their sum, and hence greater than \(49/(512Q_\Delta^2)>a_*\).

Suppose now that both endpoint energies \(F_{u_e}\) and \(F_{v_e}\) were below \(\varepsilon\). By (8), for each endpoint value \(t\in\lbrace\upsilon,\omega\rbrace\) there would be an odd integer \(a\in\lbrace1,3,\ldots,Q_\Delta\rbrace\) for which
$$
|at-1|<\sqrt{\varepsilon/a_*}=\frac1{8Q_\Delta^2}.
$$
Therefore \(|t-1/a|<1/(8Q_\Delta^2)\). Applying this to both endpoints and using their sum deviation gives two such odd integers \(a,b\) satisfying
$$
\left|\frac1a+\frac1b-1\right|
 <\frac1{8Q_\Delta^2}+\frac1{8Q_\Delta^2}+\delta
 =\frac1{2Q_\Delta^2},
$$
contrary to (10). Thus at least one of \(F_{u_e},F_{v_e},\delta_e\) is at least \(\varepsilon\). Because \(s\xi^2<1/4\) and \(256Q_\Delta^6\varepsilon=1/4\), this proves (11) in the intermediate case too.

Sum (11) over the selected high-ratio pairs and divide by \(K\). An atom's \(F_x\) is charged at most \(\Delta+1\) times: at most \(\Delta\) times as a center and at most once as an endpoint. Every source parity is the endpoint parity of at most one pair, and \(\delta_e\) is precisely \((Kr_\eta-1)^2\) for that parity. Hence the total of the \(\delta_e\) terms is at most \(K\mathcal D\). Combining (9), (11), and the low-ratio estimate proves
$$
\begin{aligned}
\beta_{\mathcal S}
 &\le256Q_\Delta^6
 \bigl[(\Delta+1)(\mathcal V_{\mathcal S}+\mathcal T_{\mathcal S})
       +\mathcal D\bigr]+2\mathcal T_{\mathcal S}\\
 &\le\bigl[256(\Delta+1)Q_\Delta^6+2\bigr]
    (\mathcal V_{\mathcal S}+2\mathcal D+\mathcal T_{\mathcal S})\\
 &=C_\Delta\mathcal E_{\mathcal S}.
\end{aligned}
$$
This is (7), including all possible overlaps of center and endpoint roles.

Next we prove the multiple-pair score price
$$
\widehat\nu\le
 R_\Delta\sum_{e\in\mathcal S}(1+\rho_e^2)\beta_e
 +T_\Delta\mathcal V_{\mathcal S}.
\tag{12}
$$
At a selected center \(x\), the identities \(p_{u_e}=s_ep_xe^{-z_e}\), \(p_{v_e}=s_ep_xe^{z_e}\) for pairs centered there give exactly
$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat V_x&=\frac2{h_x}
 \sum_{e\in\mathcal S:j_e=x}s_ez_e^2,\\
p_x\widehat H(x)^2\widehat V_x
 &=2h_xp_x^3\sum_{e\in\mathcal S:j_e=x}s_ez_e^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{13}
$$
At a center with no selected pairs the variance is zero. For one selected pair use \(\xi,\upsilon,\omega\) as above and put \(G_e=2s_eh_{j_e}\xi^3z_e^2\). Then (13) implies
$$
\widehat\nu=
 \frac{K^{-1}\sum_{e\in\mathcal S}G_e}{A_{\mathcal S}}.
\tag{14}
$$

Suppose first that \(\max(\xi,\upsilon,\omega)\le2\), and abbreviate \(s=s_e\), \(z=z_e\), \(\rho=\rho_e\). The larger endpoint is \(s\xi e^{|z|}\le2\), so \(|z|\le\rho+\log(2/\xi)\). The function \(t^2e^{-t}\) has maximum \(4/e^2\) for \(t\ge0\); setting \(t=\log(2/\xi)\) proves \(\xi\log^2(2/\xi)\le8/e^2<2\). Since \(\xi\le2\) and \(h_{j_e}\le Q_\Delta\), it follows that
$$
\begin{aligned}
G_e&\le4Q_\Delta s\xi^3
 \bigl[\rho^2+\log^2(2/\xi)\bigr]\\
 &\le8Q_\Delta s\xi^2(1+\rho^2).
\end{aligned}
\tag{15}
$$

For the other pairs let \(M=\max(\xi,\upsilon,\omega)>2\). For every \(s\in(0,1]\) and \(z\in\mathbb R\) one has
$$
z^2\le2\rho^2+4s^3\cosh(3z),\qquad \rho=\log(1/s).
\tag{16}
$$
If \(|z|\le\rho\) this is immediate. Otherwise write \(|z|=\rho+t\) with \(t>0\); then \(z^2\le2\rho^2+2t^2\), \(s^3\cosh(3z)\ge e^{3t}/2\), and \(e^{3t}\ge t^2\), the latter following from its nonnegative quadratic Taylor term. These inequalities prove (16). Also \(s\rho^2\le4/e^2<1\) and \(\upsilon^3+\omega^3=2s^3\xi^3\cosh(3z)\). Using \(h_{j_e}\le Q_\Delta\) in (16) therefore gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
G_e&\le4Q_\Delta s\rho^2\xi^3
     +4Q_\Delta s(\upsilon^3+\omega^3)\\
 &\le4Q_\Delta(\xi^3+\upsilon^3+\omega^3)
 \le12Q_\Delta M^3.
\end{aligned}
\tag{17}
$$

Choose one of this pair's center or endpoints where \(Kp_x=M\). The atom's contribution to \(K\mathcal V_{\mathcal S}\) is \(M(h_xM-1)^2\ge M(M-1)^2\ge M^3/4\), because \(h_x\ge1\) and \(M>2\). Thus (17) is paid by \(48Q_\Delta\) times that contribution. Each atom can be chosen for at most \(\Delta+1\) distinct pairs, by the center and endpoint incidence bounds. Consequently the total from (17), divided by \(K\), is at most \(48Q_\Delta(\Delta+1)\mathcal V_{\mathcal S}\). The total from (15), divided by \(K\), is at most \(8Q_\Delta\sum_{e\in\mathcal S}(1+\rho_e^2)\beta_e\). Divide these estimates by \(A_{\mathcal S}\ge1/4\) in (14). The result is (12) with exactly \(R_\Delta=32Q_\Delta\) and \(T_\Delta=192Q_\Delta(\Delta+1)\). This derivation includes all cross contributions through the full selected-row factor \(h_x\).

Assume now \(A_0<1\). Cauchy--Schwarz under the original \(p\) gives \(K\sum_xp_x^2\le\sqrt{A_0}<1\). By disjointness of all pair endpoint sets and \(2p_{u_e}p_{v_e}\le p_{u_e}^2+p_{v_e}^2\),
$$
\begin{aligned}
\zeta_{\mathcal S^c}
 &=K\sum_{e\in\mathcal P\setminus\mathcal S}p_{u_e}p_{v_e}\\
 &\le\frac K2\sum_{x\in A}p_x^2<\frac12<1.
\end{aligned}
\tag{18}
$$
Equations (4) and (6) imply \(0\le\mathcal E_{\mathcal S}<Q_\Delta^2+3\). Using \(A_{\mathcal S}\ge1/4\) and the elementary inequalities \(\log(1+t)\ge t/(1+t)\) and \(\log(1+t)\le t\) for \(t\ge0\), we obtain
$$
\begin{aligned}
\log A_{\mathcal S}
 &=\log(1+\mathcal E_{\mathcal S})
   -\log\left(1+\frac{4\zeta_{\mathcal S^c}}{A_{\mathcal S}}\right)\\
 &\ge\frac{\mathcal E_{\mathcal S}}{Q_\Delta^2+4}
    -16\zeta_{\mathcal S^c}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Since \(\mathcal E_{\mathcal S}\ge\mathcal V_{\mathcal S}\) and (7) gives \(\mathcal E_{\mathcal S}\ge\beta_{\mathcal S}/C_\Delta\), their half-sum is also a lower bound. With \(W_\Delta=2(Q_\Delta^2+4)\) and \(G_\Delta=W_\Delta C_\Delta\) this proves
$$
\log A_{\mathcal S}\ge
 \frac{\mathcal V_{\mathcal S}}{W_\Delta}
 +\frac{\beta_{\mathcal S}}{G_\Delta}
 -16\zeta_{\mathcal S^c}.
\tag{19}
$$

We choose pairs across all original factors as follows. For each factor let \(K_\ell=2^{n_\ell}\) and \(A_{0,\ell}=K_\ell^2\sum_{x\in A_\ell}p_{\ell,x}^3\). If \(A_{0,\ell}\ge1\), select no pairs in that factor. Its selected rows are all singletons, \(K_\ell^2\widehat b_\ell=A_{0,\ell}\ge1\), and \(\widehat\nu_\ell=0\).

For the remaining factors group all their pairs into global bands
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal B_k&=\left\lbrace(\ell,e):A_{0,\ell}<1,\ e\in\mathcal P_\ell,
   \ 2^{-k-1}<s_{\ell,e}\le2^{-k}\right\rbrace,\\
\beta_k&=\sum_{(\ell,e)\in\mathcal B_k}
 K_\ell s_{\ell,e}p_{\ell,j_e}^2,\\
h_k&=1+(k+1)^2(\log2)^2\qquad(k\ge0).
\end{aligned}
$$
Only finitely many bands contain pairs. Select the whole band \(\mathcal B_k\) if and only if \(\beta_k\ge D_\Delta h_k\), where \(D_\Delta=4R_\Delta G_\Delta^2\). Retain a pair exactly when its band is selected. This produces a pair subset \(\mathcal S_\ell\) in each factor, possibly retaining some and omitting others at a common center. Every selected row is still defined by (3), so all original laws and \(Z_\ell\) remain unchanged.

Put \(U=\sum_{\ell:A_{0,\ell}<1}\mathcal V_{\mathcal S_\ell}\). On band \(k\), \(\rho_{\ell,e}<(k+1)\log2\) and \(s_{\ell,e}\le2^{-k}\). Summing (12) and (19), with the nonnegative logarithms and zero variances from the other factors, yields
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{\ell=1}^L\log(K_\ell^2\widehat b_\ell)
 &\ge\frac U{W_\Delta}
    +\frac1{G_\Delta}\sum_{k\text{ selected}}\beta_k
    -16\sum_{k\text{ unselected}}2^{-k}\beta_k,\\
\sum_{\ell=1}^L\widehat\nu_\ell
 &\le T_\Delta U+R_\Delta\sum_{k\text{ selected}}h_k\beta_k.
\end{aligned}
\tag{20}
$$
In the loss term we used exactly \(\zeta_{\mathcal S_\ell^c}=\sum_{e\in\mathcal P_\ell\setminus\mathcal S_\ell}s_{\ell,e}\beta_{\ell,e}\); there is no factor proportional to the number of colliding centers.

We verify the actual-depth product conversion directly. For a supported target \(J=(j_1,\ldots,j_L)\), define
$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat R_J&=\prod_{\ell=1}^L\widehat R_{\ell,j_\ell},&
\widehat\kappa_J&=\bigotimes_{\ell=1}^L\widehat\kappa_{\ell,j_\ell},\\
\widehat Y_J(X)&=\sum_{\ell=1}^L\widehat Y_{\ell,j_\ell}(x_\ell),&
\sigma_J^2&=\sum_{\ell=1}^L\widehat V_{\ell,j_\ell}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Product factorization, (3), and the reflection symmetry of each row show
$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat H_P(J)&:=\sum_{X\in\widehat R_J}\sqrt{P_XP_{2J-X}}
 =\prod_{\ell=1}^L\widehat H_\ell(j_\ell),\\
P_X&=\widehat H_P(J)\widehat\kappa_J(X)e^{\widehat Y_J(X)}
 \qquad(X\in\widehat R_J),\\
\mathbb E_{\widehat\kappa_J}\widehat Y_J&=0,&
\mathbb E_{\widehat\kappa_J}\widehat Y_J^2&=\sigma_J^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{21}
$$
The \(\widehat H_P\) in (21) is restricted and need not equal canonical \(H_P\). The likelihood identity uses precisely the entire original \(P_X=(\prod_\ell w_{\ell,x_\ell})/(\prod_\ell Z_\ell)\).

For every closed halfspace \(\mathcal H\) in the original \(\mathbb R^N\) containing \(J\), reflection about \(J\) implies \(\mathcal H\) contains at least one endpoint of every distinct orbit \(\lbrace X,2J-X\rbrace\) in \(\widehat R_J\). It also contains \(J\). Thus, counting each noncentral orbit once and only half the available central mass,
$$
\begin{aligned}
P(\mathcal H)
 &\ge\frac12\sum_{X\in\widehat R_J}\min\lbrace P_X,P_{2J-X}\rbrace\\
 &=\frac{\widehat H_P(J)}2
   \mathbb E_{\widehat\kappa_J}e^{-|\widehat Y_J|}\\
 &\ge\frac{\widehat H_P(J)}2e^{-\sigma_J}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{22}
$$
For the last inequality, Jensen gives \(\mathbb E e^{-|Y|}\ge e^{-\mathbb E|Y|}\), and Cauchy--Schwarz gives \(\mathbb E|Y|\le\sqrt{\mathbb EY^2}=\sigma_J\). This holds for every original ambient containing halfspace without any condition on the affine dimension of the support, so it bounds \(\tau_P(J)\).

Let \(\widehat q=\bigotimes_{\ell=1}^L\widehat q_\ell\), solely as an auxiliary center law. Square (22) and average over the entire original law \(P\). The exact weight identity
$$
P_J\widehat H_P(J)^2
 =\left(\prod_{\ell=1}^L\widehat b_\ell\right)
   \prod_{\ell=1}^L\widehat q_{\ell,j_\ell}
$$
and Jensen followed by Cauchy--Schwarz give
$$
\begin{aligned}
M_2(P)&\ge\frac14\left(\prod_{\ell=1}^L\widehat b_\ell\right)
   \mathbb E_{\widehat q}e^{-2\sigma_J}\\
 &\ge\frac14\left(\prod_{\ell=1}^L\widehat b_\ell\right)
   \exp\left[-2\sqrt{\sum_{\ell=1}^L\widehat\nu_\ell}\right],
\end{aligned}
\tag{23}
$$
because \(\mathbb E_{\widehat q}\sigma_J^2=\sum_\ell\widehat\nu_\ell\). There is no change to the averaging law defining \(M_2\).

Since \(\prod_\ell K_\ell^2=4^N\), combine (20) and (23). The inequality \(\sqrt{\sum_i t_i}\le\sum_i\sqrt{t_i}\) for nonnegative \(t_i\) gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\log(4^NM_2(P))
 &\ge-\log4+\frac U{W_\Delta}-2\sqrt{T_\Delta U}\\
 &\quad+\sum_{k\text{ selected}}
   \left[\frac{\beta_k}{G_\Delta}-2\sqrt{R_\Delta h_k\beta_k}\right]
   -16\sum_{k\text{ unselected}}2^{-k}\beta_k.
\end{aligned}
\tag{24}
$$
Completing the square shows \(U/W_\Delta-2\sqrt{T_\Delta U}\ge-W_\Delta T_\Delta\). For every selected band, \(\beta_k\ge4R_\Delta G_\Delta^2h_k\), exactly the condition that makes its bracket in (24) nonnegative. For each unselected band \(\beta_k<D_\Delta h_k\). Finally,
$$
\sum_{k=0}^\infty2^{-k}h_k=2+12(\log2)^2.
$$
The two series follow from \(\sum_{k=0}^\infty t^k=(1-t)^{-1}\) and twice applying \(t\frac{d}{dt}+1\) before setting \(t=1/2\). Although only finitely many bands contain pairs, the infinite sum bounds all possible omitted-band losses. Equation (24) is therefore at least \(-\log4-W_\Delta T_\Delta-16D_\Delta\bigl(2+12(\log2)^2\bigr)=\log c_\Delta\).

This proves \(M_2(P)\ge c_\Delta4^{-N}\). Jensen under the entire original product law gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
M_3(P)
 &=\mathbb E_P\bigl[(\tau_P(J)^2)^{3/2}\bigr]\\
 &\ge\bigl[\mathbb E_P\tau_P(J)^2\bigr]^{3/2}
 =M_2(P)^{3/2},
\end{aligned}
$$
which proves the stated \(M_3\) bound. All identities and inequalities above allow empty pair selections, empty pair sets, zero score variances, and singleton supports; no step divides by a variance or requires an endpoint's own row to be a singleton. This completes the theorem.
statement:
Fix an integer \(\Delta\ge1\). Let \(L\ge1\) be an integer, and for each \(1\le\ell\le L\) let \(n_\ell\ge1\) be an integer and let \(A_\ell\subset\mathbb Z^{n_\ell}\) be finite and nonempty. Assume, separately in each factor:

1. Every coordinatewise parity class contains at most two points of \(A_\ell\).
2. The midpoint of every distinct same-parity pair in \(A_\ell\) belongs to \(A_\ell\).
3. At most \(\Delta\) distinct unordered pairs of distinct same-parity points have any one midpoint.

Here \(\Delta\) denotes the multiplicity bound called \(d\) in the registered subgoal; it does not denote the continuous dimension \(d\) of the locked problem.

Choose arbitrary weights \(w_{\ell,x}>0\) for all \(x\in A_\ell\), and retain the entire original laws and normalizers
$$
\begin{aligned}
Z_\ell&=\sum_{x\in A_\ell}w_{\ell,x},&
p_{\ell,x}&=\frac{w_{\ell,x}}{Z_\ell},&
P&=\bigotimes_{\ell=1}^L p_\ell,&
N&=\sum_{\ell=1}^L n_\ell,\\
P_{(x_1,\ldots,x_L)}&=
\frac{\prod_{\ell=1}^Lw_{\ell,x_\ell}}
     {\prod_{\ell=1}^LZ_\ell}
&&\left((x_1,\ldots,x_L)\in\prod_{\ell=1}^LA_\ell\right).
\end{aligned}
$$
Every law is zero outside its stated support. Suppose every same-parity pair \(\lbrace u,v\rbrace\) with midpoint \(j\) satisfies \(p_{\ell,j}\ge\sqrt{p_{\ell,u}p_{\ell,v}}\), equivalently \(w_{\ell,j}\ge\sqrt{w_{\ell,u}w_{\ell,v}}\). There are no other restrictions on the positive weights.

Use the canonical quantities of ee640ebdfbcb632d with their identical normalizations: for a finite law \(p\) on \(\mathbb Z^n\),
$$
\begin{aligned}
\tau_p(j)&=\inf\left\lbrace p(\mathcal H):
 \mathcal H\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is a closed halfspace containing }j
 \right\rbrace,\\
H_p(j)&=\sum_{v\in\mathbb Z^n}\sqrt{p_{j+v}p_{j-v}},&
b(p)&=\sum_jp_jH_p(j)^2,&
\chi(p)&=\sum_jp_jH_p(j),\\
M_2(p)&=\sum_jp_j\tau_p(j)^2,&
M_3(p)&=\sum_jp_j\tau_p(j)^3.
\end{aligned}
$$
Both orientations of every nonzero reflected displacement occur in \(H_p\), and zero occurs once. All halfspaces remain in the original ambient space, also for lower-dimensional supports.

With natural logarithms define the following explicit positive constants, depending only on \(\Delta\):
$$
\begin{aligned}
Q_\Delta&=2\Delta+1,&
C_\Delta&=256(\Delta+1)Q_\Delta^6+2,&
W_\Delta&=2(Q_\Delta^2+4),\\
G_\Delta&=W_\Delta C_\Delta,&
R_\Delta&=32Q_\Delta,&
T_\Delta&=192Q_\Delta(\Delta+1),\\
D_\Delta&=4R_\Delta G_\Delta^2,&
c_\Delta&=\frac14\exp\left[
 -W_\Delta T_\Delta
 -16D_\Delta\bigl(2+12(\log2)^2\bigr)\right].
\end{aligned}
$$
Then every original product above satisfies
$$
M_2(P)\ge c_\Delta4^{-N},\qquad
M_3(P)\ge c_\Delta^{3/2}8^{-N}.
$$
The constant \(c_\Delta\) is independent of all dimensions, supports, weights, normalizers, and the number of factors. Empty sets of nontrivial pairs and singleton factors are permitted.
